subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in the metal hydride NaH?
questions.explain: In metal hydrides hydrogen is −1 (the metal Na is +1).

questions.q: The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
questions.explain: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

questions.q: When solid NaCl dissolves, the enthalpy of solution equals:
options: Lattice dissociation enthalpy + sum of hydration enthalpies
questions.explain: ΔHsol = ΔH(lattice dissociation, +) + ΣΔH(hydration, −).

questions.q: Removing product continuously from an equilibrium system causes the equilibrium to:
options: shift to the right to replace the product
questions.explain: By Le Chatelier, removing product drives the reaction forward to partially replace what was removed.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines the standard enthalpy of formation of a compound?
options: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous atoms is formed from an element
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of water is formed in a neutralisation reaction
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is burned completely in oxygen
questions.explain: ΔHf is defined as forming 1 mol of compound from its constituent elements in their standard states.

questions.q: Which Cu electron configuration is correct, reflecting the stability of a full d sub-shell?
questions.explain: Copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 because a completely full 3d sub-shell with a single 4s electron is energetically favourable.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a system at equilibrium. What happens to the position of equilibrium?
options: It shifts towards the exothermic direction
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not shift the equilibrium position.

questions.q: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, what is the effect of increasing the total pressure?
options: No change because moles are equal on both sides
The position of equilibrium shifts to the left
The position of equilibrium shifts to the right
questions.explain: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (2 vs 4), i.e. towards NH₃ on the right.

questions.q: Using ΔHf, the enthalpy of a reaction is calculated as:
questions.explain: ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants).

questions.q: The purpose of the salt bridge in an electrochemical cell is to:
options: complete the circuit and maintain electrical neutrality
questions.explain: The salt bridge allows ions to flow to balance charge and complete the circuit; electrons flow through the wire.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the permanganate ion, MnO₄⁻?
questions.explain: With O at −2 (×4 = −8) and overall charge −1, Mn must be +7.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ weak acid (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.20 mol dm⁻³ of its salt. The pH is:
questions.explain: With [acid] = [salt], [H⁺] = Ka = 10⁻⁵, so pH = pKa = 5.0.

questions.q: For the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, the conventional cell representation places the:
options: salt bridge on the far left
more negative electrode (Zn) on the left
more positive electrode (Cu) on the left
questions.explain: By IUPAC convention the more negative (oxidation) half-cell is written on the left.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state, such as O2(g)?
options: Equal to its enthalpy of atomisation
questions.explain: By definition an element in its standard state has ΔHf = 0.

questions.q: Oxidation is best defined in terms of oxidation number as:
questions.explain: Oxidation corresponds to a loss of electrons and therefore an increase in oxidation number.

questions.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
questions.explain: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus.

questions.q: Which factors increase the magnitude (more exothermic) of a lattice enthalpy?
options: Smaller ionic radii and larger ionic charges
Larger ionic radii and smaller charges
questions.explain: Smaller, more highly charged ions give greater electrostatic attraction and a more exothermic lattice enthalpy.

questions.q: Why is the second ionisation energy of any element always greater than its first?
options: Shielding increases after the first electron is removed
The nuclear charge increases after ionisation
The second electron is removed from a positive ion, so it is held more strongly by the same nuclear charge over fewer electrons
The second electron is removed from a larger atom
questions.explain: After the first electron leaves, the remaining electrons are pulled in by an unchanged nuclear charge with reduced repulsion, so more energy is needed.

questions.q: What is the relative charge and relative mass of an electron (to the usual approximation)?
questions.explain: An electron has a relative charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836 of a proton.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 is:
questions.explain: With ΔH negative and ΔS positive, ΔG is negative at all temperatures.

questions.q: The mole fraction of a gas is 0.25 and the total pressure is 200 kPa. Its partial pressure is:
questions.explain: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.25 × 200 = 50 kPa.

questions.q: The standard conditions for measuring a standard electrode potential are:
options: 298 K, 200 kPa, and 2.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions
273 K, 101 kPa, and 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solutions
373 K, 100 kPa, and 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions
298 K, 100 kPa, and 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions
questions.explain: Standard electrode potentials are quoted at 298 K, 100 kPa and 1.0 mol dm⁻³ ion concentrations.

questions.q: What is the main reason first ionisation energy generally decreases down a group?
options: Nuclear charge decreases down the group
Electron-electron repulsion decreases down the group
The outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and more shielded, despite increased nuclear charge
questions.explain: Down a group the outer electron occupies a higher principal energy level and experiences more shielding, so it is held less strongly even though nuclear charge rises.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of a molecule, which peak corresponds to the molecular ion?
options: The peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring isotope peaks), equal to the relative molecular mass
The peak at the lowest m/z value
questions.explain: The molecular ion peak is the one at the highest m/z (the M peak), and its value equals the relative molecular mass.

questions.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element show a large jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies. In which group does the element lie?
questions.explain: A big jump after two electrons are removed shows the third electron comes from an inner, closer shell, identifying a Group 2 element.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle, the lattice enthalpy of formation refers to:
options: Breaking 1 mol of ionic lattice into gaseous ions
Forming 1 mol of ionic lattice from gaseous ions (exothermic)
questions.explain: Lattice enthalpy of formation is the exothermic formation of the lattice from gaseous ions.

questions.q: Why do bond-enthalpy calculations give only approximate ΔH values?
options: They only apply to ionic compounds
Bond enthalpies are exact for each molecule
They assume the reaction is at 0 K
Mean bond enthalpies are averages and ignore the specific molecular environment
questions.explain: Mean values are averaged over many compounds, so they differ slightly from any specific molecule.

questions.q: Which change alters the value of the equilibrium constant Kc for a given reaction?
options: Changing the concentration of a reactant
questions.explain: Only a change in temperature changes the value of Kc; concentration, pressure and catalysts do not.

questions.q: A buffer has [acid] = 0.10 and [salt] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Using [H⁺] = Ka × [acid]/[salt], pH is approximately:
How many orbitals are present in a p sub-shell, and what shape are they?
questions.explain: A p sub-shell has three dumb-bell-shaped orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles to each other.
